\section[o impacto]{o impacto — the impact}

\label{lesson:PT-C351-impacto}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to give rise to, then the Portuguese for thanks to.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o impacto}
\textbf{o impacto} — \textquotedblleft{}the impact\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A nova fábrica teve um grande impacto na aldeia.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The new factory had a big impact on the village.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Ter impacto em} — to have an impact on.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{impacto} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{impāctus} (EtymDB), the participle of \emph{impingere} \textquotedblleft{}to push, to strike or drive into\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), built from \emph{in} and \emph{pangere} \textquotedblleft{}to fix\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o impacto}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o impacto}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{o impacto}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to give rise to, then the Portuguese for thanks to, then say \emph{o impacto} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does o impacto mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The impact\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a repercussão]{a repercussão — the repercussion, the knock-on effect}

\label{lesson:PT-C351-repercussao}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for thanks to, then the Portuguese for the impact.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a repercussão}
\textbf{a repercussão} — \textquotedblleft{}the repercussion, the knock-on effect\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A decisão teve repercussões em todo o país.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The decision had repercussions across the whole country.}
\end{quote}

Mostly plural: \emph{as repercussões}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{repercussão} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{repercussiō} \textquotedblleft{}a rebounding, a reflection\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB, Lewis \& Short), from \emph{repercutere} \textquotedblleft{}to strike back\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{quatere} \textquotedblleft{}to shake, to strike\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a repercussão}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{a repercussão}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{a repercussão}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for thanks to, then the Portuguese for the impact, then say \emph{a repercussão} again
\end{itemize}

\section[implicar]{implicar — to involve, to entail; to imply}

\label{lesson:PT-C351-implicar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the impact, then the Portuguese for the repercussion.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: implicar}
\textbf{implicar} — \textquotedblleft{}to involve, to entail; to imply\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mudar de casa implica muito trabalho.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Moving house involves a lot of work.}
\end{quote}

Informally, \emph{implicar com alguém} — to pick on someone.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{implicar} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{implicāre} \textquotedblleft{}to fold into, to entangle\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB, Lewis \& Short), built from \emph{in} and \emph{plicāre} \textquotedblleft{}to fold\textquotedblright{}; the inherited form of the same Latin verb is \emph{empregar}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{implicar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{implicar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{implicar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the impact, then the Portuguese for the repercussion, then say \emph{implicar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[acarretar]{acarretar — to entail, to bring about}

\label{lesson:PT-C351-acarretar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the repercussion, then the Portuguese for to involve.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: acarretar}
\textbf{acarretar} — \textquotedblleft{}to entail, to bring about\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Esse erro acarretou muitos problemas à empresa.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{That mistake brought many problems to the company.}
\end{quote}

Formal; close to \emph{implicar}. \emph{Acarretar custos} — to entail costs.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{acarretar} first meant \textquotedblleft{}to carry by cart\textquotedblright{}: it is built on \emph{carreta} \textquotedblleft{}small cart\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{carro}, inherited from Latin \emph{carrus} \textquotedblleft{}a wagon\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[desencadear]{desencadear — to trigger, to unleash}

\label{lesson:PT-C351-desencadear}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to involve, then the Portuguese for to entail.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: desencadear}
\textbf{desencadear} — \textquotedblleft{}to trigger, to unleash\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Uma pequena discussão desencadeou uma grande zanga.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{A small argument triggered a big row.}
\end{quote}

Literally to unchain.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{desencadear} is built from \emph{des-} and \emph{encadear} \textquotedblleft{}to chain\textquotedblright{}, on \emph{cadeia} \textquotedblleft{}chain\textquotedblright{}, inherited from Latin \emph{catēna} \textquotedblleft{}a chain\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): to let loose from the chain.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
